headline: Middle East energy shock only ~2.5% of AU CPI basket directly, but second-round effects through construction costs, rents and business pass-through are the real inflation risk
reasoning: Pelosi notes that automotive fuel (including diesel) is only around 2.5% of the Australian CPI basket, so the direct impact of the Middle Eastern oil shock is limited. The more important concern is how higher energy input costs feed through to construction costs, housing supply, and rents, and whether businesses with unrelenting demand are forced to pass on higher costs more broadly. Australia entered the crisis already dealing with sticky and elevated underlying inflation, compounding the risk. The RBA will be focused on whether this relative price shock becomes a generalised inflationary problem.
quote: if we look squarely at the diesel story, I think that's important. But particularly given the margin issues we've had there between the wholesale and retail prices and diesel. Diesel costs, as everyone's probably aware, have really been quite elevated and remaining sticky on that, sort of that, on that spike. Uh, look, if we take all in all energy costs and particularly automotive fuel costs in Australia, when we look at the CPI basket, it's only around 2.5% of the basket... I think the more important issue for us is how does it actually feed into other parts of production, other inflationary impulses... we already had a sticky and elevated underlying inflation problem to begin with that pre-dated the Middle Eastern crisis.
episode_title: The inflation threat that could change the RBA’s next move

headline: US 10-year at 24-year highs with ~100bps rise in two months; MOVE index rising sharply while VIX signals equity complacency — a dangerous dislocation; bond level normalisation makes sense but volatility is troubling
reasoning: Pelosi highlights that US 10-year Treasury yields have risen approximately 100 basis points over roughly two months, reaching 24-year highs, constituting a significant bond rout. He notes a dislocation between the MOVE index (bond market volatility equivalent of VIX), which is rising precipitously, and the equity VIX, which suggests equity markets remain complacent. He frames the current yield level as a return to normalcy after the aberration of the post-GFC era, comparing it to 2005-2006 levels, but is troubled by the pace of the move and what the elevated uncertainty in bond markets implies for equities.
quote: right now we're seeing a bit of a dislocation or, or a there's a there's a conundrum building up here. And I think on one hand, you know, measures like the move index, which is something I focus on, which is, I guess, the the bond market equivalent of the, the VIX for the equities, that is, that's starting to rise quite precipitously. And at the same time, the VIX and the equity market volatility would suggest that the markets the equity markets at least are somewhat complacent... bond yields have risen in the US, something like 100 points in the last, uh, 6 to 2, roughly two months, 100 basis points. And that's, that's that's quite meaningful. Um, I mean, I would step back and just say a couple of things very quickly on this one. We should try and sort of, uh, throw out the last 15 years as a guide here. That was really in my mind, the aberration. And we're getting back to something that looks a little bit more normal. So those early 2000 years now, 2005, 2006. This is where we're getting back to. So from that standpoint, the levels kind of make sense to me. Well, what is a little bit troubling here is the volatility and what that actually tells us.

headline: RBA on the right path tightening, but may need to do more if second-round inflation effects persist; currency channel and construction/housing rents are key transmission risks
reasoning: Pelosi explains that high oil prices tend to weaken the Australian dollar, creating an import inflation problem on top of direct energy costs. The more concerning channels are material and construction cost increases, which restrict housing supply and push rents higher, as well as broader business cost pass-through to consumers. He believes the RBA is focused on these second-round effects and that financial conditions continuing to tighten is the right approach, but questions remain about whether more needs to be done to bring visible evidence of generalised inflation being addressed.
quote: there's obviously the currency channel, you know, high oil prices tends to tends to also flow through to a weakening the Aussie dollar. We have seen that many times. So you get this import inflation problem. Uh but there are other channels that are perhaps more concerning from, from my part. And, you know, the way he feeds into particularly material costs, construction costs and what that means for housing. And of course, if housing becomes a lot more difficult to deliver in terms of supply, then what does that mean for rents?... I think as we see financial conditions tightening continue to tighten. I think they're on the right path there. The question is whether they need to do more to get us some visible evidence that that generalised inflationary problem is being addressed.

headline: US bond yields up ~100bps in two months; volatility and fat tail risks are troubling, but equity markets yet to reprice — watching credit spreads, VIX and equity breadth for confirmation of stress
reasoning: Pelosi notes US bond yields have risen roughly 100 basis points over the past two months, which he sees as a return to more 'normal' pre-GFC levels (2005-2006 era) rather than something alarming in level terms. However, the volatility itself is worrying: the MOVE index is signalling significant uncertainty about where rates could go, and tail risks are becoming fat. He observes that investors are demanding higher term premium as compensation for holding long-duration bonds. Despite this, equity markets have not yet repriced: the VIX remains depressed, credit spreads are contained, and equity market breadth has not deteriorated. He is watching for widening credit spreads, a VIX spike, and breadth/depth deterioration in equities as signals that the higher discount rate and cost of funds will bite.
quote: What is a little bit troubling here is the volatility and what that actually tells us. And that there's clearly uncertainty, uh, sort of playing out here because that that move index is really highlighting the, the bond markets, uh, sort of associated uncertainty with respect to where rates could go. And the tail risks are now really increasing. They're getting quite fat. So what that suggests to me is that the market either needs to look for evidence that how they're going to be compensated to some extent. The compensation is coming through higher term premium in the bond market. So investors are seeking a lot more compensation and buying long duration bonds. But at the same time, we haven't really seen this spill over into the equity market. Why isn't. Why is it the case of the VIX continues to remain depressed. Why is it that credit spreads are still fairly contained. And the other thing I'm watching for is why aren't we seeing a breather a more, um, a more sort of, uh, issues to sort of develop across the breadth of the equity market. So these are the things I'm looking for. I'm looking for widening credit spreads. The VIX, the potential spike here and some deterioration across the breadth and depth of the equity market.
